questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: I _____ (play) football every Sunday with my friends.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'every Sunday' indicates a habitual or regular action in the present. Therefore, the simple present tense 'play' is the correct choice.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: She _____ (go) to the supermarket yesterday evening.
questions.explanation: The time marker 'yesterday evening' clearly indicates an action that was completed in the past. Therefore, the simple past tense 'went' is correct.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: By the time the police finally arrived, the clever thief _____ (escape).
questions.explanation: When two actions happen in the past, the action that happens first takes the past perfect tense ('had escaped'), and the subsequent action takes the simple past ('arrived').

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: I _____ (work) continuously on this difficult project since 8 AM this morning.
questions.explanation: The preposition 'since' along with a time reference (8 AM) indicates an action that started in the past and is still continuing in the present. This requires the present perfect continuous tense 'have been working'.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: If you had told me about the serious problem earlier, I _____ (help) you.
questions.explanation: This is a Type 3 conditional sentence (unreal past condition). The 'if' clause uses the past perfect ('had told'), so the main clause must use 'would have' + past participle ('would have helped').

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: Look at those incredibly dark clouds! It _____ (rain) very heavily soon.
questions.explanation: When making a prediction based on present, visible evidence (dark clouds), the 'be going to' form is used rather than 'will'.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: Hardly had I reached the busy railway station when the express train _____ (leave).
questions.explanation: In the 'Hardly had... when...' construction, the first clause takes the past perfect ('had reached') and the subordinate 'when' clause takes the simple past ('left').

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: The Maharaja of Mysore _____ (own) this magnificent palace since the early twentieth century.
questions.explanation: 'Own' is a stative verb and cannot be used in any continuous form. For a state that began in the past and continues up to the present, the Present Perfect ('has owned') is required. Options A and D wrongly force a stative verb into the continuous aspect. Option C (Past Perfect) implies ownership has already ended, which contradicts the open timeframe signalled by 'since the early twentieth century'.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: By the time the last train departs tonight, the station staff _____ (serve) over five hundred passengers.

options.option_text: will be serving over five hundred passengers
will have served over five hundred passengers
would have served over five hundred passengers
will serve over five hundred passengers

questions.explanation: 'By the time + a future reference point' signals an action that will be fully completed before that future moment, requiring the Future Perfect ('will have served'). Option A (Future Continuous) shows an action still in progress, not concluded. Option C (Conditional Perfect) is reserved for hypothetical past scenarios, not future timelines. Option D (Simple Future) loses the critical 'completion before a deadline' meaning that the structure demands.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: The geography teacher explained to the students that the river Ganga _____ (originate) from the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand.

options.option_text: had originated from the Gangotri glacier
was originating from the Gangotri glacier
would originate from the Gangotri glacier

questions.explanation: Statements of universal, scientific, or geographical fact retain the Simple Present tense even in reported speech — no tense backshift is applied. Option A (Past Perfect) is the most tempting distractor because learners mechanically backshift all verbs in indirect speech; however, since the Ganga's origin from Gangotri is a permanent geographical truth, 'originates' remains correct. Option C misuses the continuous form; Option D introduces an unreal conditional meaning.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: The Reserve Bank of India _____ (announce) a surprise cut in the repo rate just a few moments ago.

options.option_text: announced a surprise cut in the repo rate
has announced a surprise cut in the repo rate
had announced a surprise cut in the repo rate
was announcing a surprise cut in the repo rate

questions.explanation: In standard British English (the norm for SSC and Banking exam answer keys), 'just a few moments ago' combined with a result still relevant to the present triggers the Present Perfect ('has announced'). Option A (Simple Past) is acceptable in American English but is marked incorrect in Indian exam patterns when present relevance is implied. Option C (Past Perfect) requires a prior past reference point. Option D (Past Continuous) wrongly implies the announcement was interrupted.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank using the correct verb form: The examination board stipulated that each candidate _____ (submit) their admit card at the entry gate without fail.

options.option_text: submits their admit card at the entry gate
submit their admit card at the entry gate
submitted their admit card at the entry gate
would submit their admit card at the entry gate

questions.explanation: After verbs of demand, stipulation, or recommendation (stipulate, insist, recommend, require), the mandative subjunctive rule applies: the verb takes the base form regardless of the subject. So 'each candidate submit' is correct, not 'submits'. Option A adds a third-person '-s', violating the subjunctive rule. Option C uses Simple Past, implying the action is complete history. Option D introduces an unnecessary conditional nuance not required by 'stipulated that'.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: The archaeologists _____ (excavate) the ancient Indus Valley site for three years when they finally discovered the rare bronze figurine.

options.option_text: were excavating the ancient Indus Valley site
have been excavating the ancient Indus Valley site
had been excavating the ancient Indus Valley site
excavated that ancient Indus Valley site entirely

questions.explanation: The sentence describes a continuous activity ('for three years') that was ongoing up to and immediately before a completed past event ('discovered'). This dual requirement — duration + completion before another past action — is the precise use case of the Past Perfect Continuous ('had been excavating'). Option A (Past Continuous) cannot carry the 'for three years' durational emphasis preceding a discovery. Option B (Present Perfect Continuous) wrongly connects the action to the present. Option D (Simple Past) strips away the sense of sustained effort that preceded the find.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatically correct sentence with proper negative fronting and tense structure.

options.option_text: Not once did the veteran diplomat revealed his true intentions during the summit.
Not once did the veteran diplomat reveal his true intentions during the summit.
Not once had the veteran diplomat reveal his true intentions during the summit.
Not once the veteran diplomat did reveal his true intentions during the summit.

questions.explanation: After a negative adverbial ('Not once'), subject-auxiliary inversion is mandatory, and the main verb must be in the base form: 'Not once + auxiliary + subject + base verb'. Option A wrongly uses 'revealed' (past participle/past tense) after 'did' instead of the base form 'reveal' — the most common error here. Option C uses 'had' as auxiliary but then incorrectly pairs it with the base form 'reveal' instead of the required past participle 'revealed'. Option D places the auxiliary 'did' after the subject, destroying the inversion structure entirely.

questions.stem: The production team _____ the entire documentary thrice before they submitted it to the international film festival committee.
questions.explanation: B is correct because the watching was completed before another past action ('submitted'), which demands past perfect 'had watched'. A ('has watched') is wrong because present perfect cannot refer to an action that clearly preceded a completed past event — it would need a past perfect, not a present one.

questions.stem: By the time the rescue team reaches the stranded mountaineers, the survivors _____ for nearly forty-eight hours without food or water.

options.option_text: will have been waiting (future perfect continuous)

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'By the time X [present simple for future], Y will have been doing Z' uses the future perfect continuous to show an action of specific duration extending up to a future reference point. B ('would have waited') is wrong because conditional perfect implies a hypothetical or unfulfilled past situation, not an open future one.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly applies the rule that stative verbs denoting mental states cannot be used in continuous tenses?

options.option_text: The judge is believing the defendant's alibi without question.
The judge believes the defendant's alibi without question.
The judge was believing the alibi presented in the court.
The judge has been believing this alibi for some time.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'believe' is a stative verb expressing a mental state and cannot take continuous forms. Options A, C, and D incorrectly force 'believe' into continuous constructions (is believing, was believing, has been believing). A common trap is D, where 'has been believing' sounds advanced but violates the stative verb rule.

questions.stem: The principal announced to the students, 'You will attend a special workshop tomorrow.' In reported speech, this correctly becomes: 'The principal announced that _____.'

options.option_text: they will attend a special workshop tomorrow
you would attend a special workshop the next day
they would attend a special workshop the next day
they would have attended a workshop the next day

questions.explanation: C is correct because reported speech requires three simultaneous changes here: (1) 'will' backshifts to 'would'; (2) the address pronoun 'you' shifts to 'they' since the reporter is external; (3) the time adverbial 'tomorrow' shifts to 'the next day'. B fails by retaining 'you' without pronoun change. D incorrectly uses 'would have attended' (conditional perfect), which distorts the original meaning.

questions.stem: The village health worker informed the doctor that the patient _____ from severe dehydration since the previous night.
questions.explanation: C is correct because when the reporting verb 'informed' is in the past, present perfect continuous ('has been suffering') must backshift to past perfect continuous ('had been suffering'). 'Since the previous night' confirms an ongoing duration up to a past reference point, requiring the continuous form. A is the most tempting distractor but present tenses cannot survive intact under past-tense reported speech.

questions.stem: An economist wrote in her 2019 paper: 'If the government implements these fiscal measures, inflation will fall significantly.' Correctly reported in indirect speech, this reads: 'The economist wrote that _____.'

options.option_text: if the government implemented those measures, inflation would fall significantly
if the government had implemented those measures, inflation would have fallen
if the government implements those measures, inflation will fall significantly
if the government would implement the measures, inflation would significantly fall

questions.explanation: A is correct: a Type 1 conditional ('implements...will fall') becomes a Type 2 structure in past-tense reported speech — 'implemented...would fall' (present simple → past simple; will → would). B is the critical trap — it converts the sentence to a Type 3 conditional, implying the measures were never implemented, which fundamentally distorts the original assertion. C wrongly retains present tenses without the required backshift.

questions.stem: By 2030, if current deforestation trends in the Eastern Himalayas continue unchecked, the region _____ nearly half of its endemic plant species permanently.

options.option_text: will have lost (future perfect — completion by 2030)
would have lost (conditional perfect — wrong type)
will lose (simple future — misses deadline sense)
has lost (present perfect — wrong future reference)

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'By 2030' signals a future deadline by which an action will be fully completed, requiring future perfect 'will have lost'. The Type 1 conditional 'if...continue' (present simple) takes a future perfect in the result clause to capture completion by the deadline — simple future 'will lose' (C) omits this completion sense. B ('would have lost') is wrong because conditional perfect applies to hypothetical past scenarios, not open future conditionals.
